content: These events can occur suddenly and without prior warning, potentially leading to fatal outcomes. The risk of such events may be elevated in individuals who use NSAIDs for extended periods. Inform your doctor if you or any family members have a history of heart disease, heart attack, or stroke, if you smoke, or if you have or have had high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or diabetes. Seek emergency medical attention immediately if you experience symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. If you are scheduled to undergo coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, do not take fenoprofen immediately before or after the procedure. NSAIDs, including fenoprofen, can cause ulcers, bleeding, or perforations in the stomach or intestines. These complications can arise at any time during treatment, often without warning, and may result in death. The risk is higher for individuals who take NSAIDs long-term, are older, have poor health, or consume large amounts of alcohol while taking fenoprofen. Inform your doctor if you are taking any of the following medications: anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), or oral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone, methylprednisolone, prednisone). Additionally, let your doctor know if you have or have had ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other bleeding disorders. If you experience symptoms such as stomach pain, heartburn, vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds, blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools, stop taking fenoprofen and contact your doctor immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for monitoring. Your doctor will carefully observe your symptoms and may order tests to evaluate your body’s response to fenoprofen. Communicate openly with your doctor about how you are feeling so they can adjust your medication dosage to minimize the risk of serious side effects. Your doctor or pharmacist will provide you with a Medication Guide when you start fenoprofen and each time you refill your prescription. Read this information thoroughly and ask any questions you may have. You can also visit the FDA or the manufacturer’s website for additional details. Fenoprofen is prescribed to alleviate pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness associated with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. It is also used to manage mild to moderate pain from other causes. Fenoprofen belongs to a class of drugs called NSAIDs, which work by inhibiting the production of substances in the body that cause pain, fever, and inflammation. Fenoprofen is available in capsule and tablet forms for oral administration. It is typically taken with a full glass of water three to four times daily for arthritis or every 4–6 hours as needed for pain. To reduce stomach upset, fenoprofen can be taken with meals, milk, or an antacid if recommended by your doctor. If you take fenoprofen regularly, try to take it at the same times each day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Do not take more or less of the medication or take it more frequently than prescribed. If you are using fenoprofen for arthritis, you may notice symptom improvement within a few days, but it may take 2–3 weeks or longer to experience the full benefits. Fenoprofen is also used to treat ankylosing spondylitis and gouty arthritis and may sometimes be prescribed to reduce fever. Discuss the risks of using this medication with your doctor. Fenoprofen may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking fenoprofen, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to fenoprofen, aspirin, other NSAIDs, or any inactive ingredients in fenoprofen capsules. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. Mention medications listed in the Important Warning section, as well as ACE inhibitors, diuretics, lithium, oral diabetes medications, methotrexate, phenobarbital, phenytoin, and sulfa antibiotics. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you closely for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have or have had conditions mentioned in the Important Warning section, asthma (especially with nasal polyps), swelling in the extremities, hearing impairment, anemia, or liver or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking fenoprofen, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking fenoprofen. Be aware that this medication may cause drowsiness; avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you. Alcohol can exacerbate drowsiness caused by fenoprofen, so avoid consuming alcohol while taking this medication. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking fenoprofen. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Fenoprofen may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience headache, nervousness, drowsiness, sweating, constipation, or ringing in the ears, especially if these symptoms persist or worsen. Serious side effects require immediate medical attention and include blurred vision, uncontrollable shaking, unexplained weight gain, fever, blisters, rash, itching, hives, swelling, hoarseness, difficulty breathing or swallowing, yellowing of the skin or eyes, extreme fatigue, unusual bleeding or bruising, lack of energy, stomach pain, flu-like symptoms, pale skin, rapid heartbeat, discolored or bloody urine, back pain, or painful urination. Stop taking fenoprofen and contact your doctor if you experience any of these symptoms. Store fenoprofen in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include heartburn, upset stomach, vomiting, stomach pain, dizziness, unsteadiness, headache, ringing in the ears, uncontrollable shaking, drowsiness, and confusion. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
